extracted.intended_audience: pro se patent applicants (independent inventors and small businesses filing without an attorney/agent)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and filing U.S. patent applications by applicants filing without a registered patent attorney or agent, covering provisional and nonprovisional applications, required content, filing procedures, amendment rules, fees, and available USPTO assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a registered patent attorney or agent (recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO always recommends using a registered patent attorney or agent to assist in preparing your application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not required, the USPTO recognizes cost barriers and provides Pro Se Assistance resources; USPTO employees cannot give legal advice. The recommendation reflects that skilled preparation and prosecution largely determine a patent's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three types of patent applications that can be filed: utility, design, and plant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility: new and useful process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or improvements (see Utility Patent Application Guide). Design: new, original, ornamental design for an article of manufacture (see Design Patent Application Guide). Plant: invents or discovers and asexually reproduces a distinct and new variety of plant (see Plant Patent Application Guide). Utility protects how an article is used and works; design protects how it looks; both can be obtained for the same article if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (novelty, non-obviousness, utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: New (novelty), non-obvious, and useful are required for utility patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New (novelty): the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in 35 U.S.C. 102. Non-obvious: differences between the claimed invention and prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would not have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art. Useful (utility): invention accomplishes something or works; utility must be well-established, and a person of ordinary skill must immediately appreciate why the invention is useful. Utility must be specific, substantial, and credible. See MPEP sections referenced for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent subject matter exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be obtained for laws of nature, physical phenomena, abstract ideas, or a mere idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete description of the actual machine or other subject matter for which a patent is sought is required. Literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works cannot be patented (may be copyrightable). See MPEP section 2106 I for up-to-date eligibility guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to determine if an invention is patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Review what can and cannot be patented, the description of patent types, and learn the basics of the patent process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for previous public disclosures (prior art) including U.S. patents and patent application publications, foreign patents, and printed publications. While prior art search is not required before filing, it is advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art search guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct a prior art search to identify pertinent prior art and previous public disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Public Search Facility, Patent and Trademark Resource Centers (PTRCs), web tutorials like 'How to conduct a preliminary search', and the '7-Step U.S. Patent Search Strategy Guide'. A registered attorney or agent may also perform a search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application definition and pendency
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional application is a U.S. national application filed for utility and plant inventions that serves as a placeholder to establish an early effective filing date for a later nonprovisional application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional applications: pendency lasts 12 months (non-extendable), are not examined, and must be followed by a corresponding nonprovisional application within 12 months to benefit from the earlier filing date and to retain 'patent pending' status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for filing a provisional application
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional application must include a detailed written description of the invention including drawings (if necessary), title, inventor names and residences, correspondence address, indication of any U.S. government agency interest, filing fees, and a cover sheet or form PTO/SB/16 (or ADS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a filing date may be obtained without drawings, applicants shall furnish drawings necessary for understanding the subject matter. A provisional application filing guide is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonprovisional application definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonprovisional patent application is an application examined by a patent examiner and may be issued as a patent if patentability requirements are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonprovisional applications must include a specification providing a detailed written description, drawings when necessary, claim(s), abstract of the disclosure, and title. See MPEP section 601 I for further details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required documents and forms for nonprovisional filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonprovisional applications require specific forms and documents such as the Utility Patent Application Transmittal form (PTO/AIA/15), Application Data Sheet (PTO/AIA/14), appropriate fees (see fee schedule), Fee Transmittal form PTO/SB/17, and an executed Oath or Declaration (form PTO/AIA/01 or PTO/AIA/08).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nonprovisional application filing guide is available. Ensure correct forms, fees, and executed documents are included to avoid missing parts or incomplete application notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and content of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim defines the scope of the invention; it must particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter regarded as the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One or more claims may be presented in dependent form, referring back to and further limiting another claim(s) in the same application. The claim(s) determine the limits of patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting format requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim should be a single sentence, and where a claim sets forth multiple elements or steps, each element or step should be separated by a line indentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For further details see Claim(s) at 37 C.F.R. 1.75. The USPTO provides Inventor Info Chat presentations on claim drafting including basic structure, examples, and questions to ask regarding your invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting substance (questions and approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use available claim-drafting guidance and a structured approach (e.g., ask questions about the invention when drafting a claim set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office of Innovation Development holds presentations (Inventor Info Chat) that include examples, questions to ask, and one approach to claim drafting to help pro se applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: At least one drawing is required if it is necessary for understanding the subject matter to be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants are advised to file any drawings necessary for understanding the invention with the application. See MPEP section 608.02 for details on drawing content and standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and entity status
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application is subject to a basic filing fee and additional fees including a search fee, examination fee, and issue fee; fees vary with type, content, size of application and entity status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may obtain fee reductions based on entity status (small entity or micro entity) by meeting certain requirements. All payments must be in U.S. dollars and in accepted payment forms; specific rules apply to credit card information and liability. See fee schedule and MPEP section 509 for fee completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted payment methods
rubrics_metrics.description: All fee payments shall be made in U.S. dollars and in the form of cashier’s or certified check, treasury note, national bank notes, USPS money order, or credit card.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment by credit card must specify the amount and necessary information; the USPTO will not accept a general authorization to charge a credit card, and is not liable if a credit card number becomes public when not provided on the USPTO Credit Card Payment form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to file an application (filing channels)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application can be filed via USPS mail, hand delivery to the USPTO, or electronically via Patent Center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic filing via Patent Center avoids the non-electronic filing fee for utility applications (an additional fee applies to mailed/hand-delivered utility applications). Patent Center requires a registered user to file and pay; most new electronic applications can be viewed within an hour and an application number is assigned immediately upon filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-electronic filing fee and Patent Center notes
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional non-electronic filing fee will be charged to applications mailed or hand-delivered (not charged for design, plant, and provisional applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic filing is the only way to avoid the non-electronic filing fee for utility applications. Plant applications and related documents are not permitted to be filed via Patent Center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Missing Parts and Notice of Incomplete Application
rubrics_metrics.description: A Notice of Missing Parts is sent when an essential filing requirement is missing; a Notice of Incomplete Application is sent when nonprovisional application papers are deemed incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of essential filing requirements include appropriate filing fees, improper entity status, and improper priority claims. Essential filing papers include the specification, drawings, and claims. The filing date will be the date corrections are made. See MPEP section 506 and related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to amend the specification (format and no new matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to the specification requires a marked-up copy, a clean copy, and a statement that the amendment does not contain new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marked-up copy: underline additions and strike through deletions. Clean copy: the new specification as it should read. Statement of no new matter must accompany a substitute specification. New matter may not be added irrespective of whether the statement is included (37 CFR 1.121(f)). Examples are provided in guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to amend claims (format and status indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to claims must show added text by underlining and deleted text by strike-through (or double brackets if strike-through is not perceivable); the status of every claim must be indicated after its claim number with identifiers like (Original), (Currently amended), (Canceled), (Withdrawn), (Previously presented), (New), (Not entered).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New claims may be added with the status 'New'. When an entire claim is canceled, its text should not be presented and the status should be 'Canceled'.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to amend drawings (replacement sheets and labeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes to drawings must be submitted on a replacement sheet labeled 'Replacement Sheet' and must include all figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet; any new sheet with an additional figure must be labeled 'New Sheet'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All changes to drawings must be explained in detail in the drawing amendment or remarks section of the amendment paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition to revive an unintentionally abandoned application
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition, along with all necessary fees, must be filed to revive an unintentionally abandoned application using form PTO/SB/64.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions may be filed via USPS or as an ePetition; ePetition offers benefits like secure filing with auto-grant, faster decisions when immediate petition decisions are needed, and increased accuracy via immediate feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited examination options
rubrics_metrics.description: Several programs allow earlier examination: Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH), Track One prioritized examination, and petitions to make special (e.g., based on age).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PPH speeds examination of corresponding applications in participating offices when at least one claim has been allowed; no fee required. Track One (utility nonprovisional and plant only) requires an additional fee, aims for final disposition within 12 months of grant, and is limited to 12,000 requests per fiscal year (not available for design patents). Petition to make special based on age advances examination for applicants at least 65 years old and has no fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available USPTO assistance resources
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO provides multiple assistance services: Inventors Assistance Center (IAC), Pro Se Assistance Center, Application Assistance Unit (AAU), Patent Pro Bono Program, and Law School Clinic Certification Program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IAC staffed by former supervisory/primary examiners and attorneys answers general questions. Pro Se Assistance Center provides one-on-one assistance, webinars, and appointment-based help. AAU assists with pre-examination and post-examination processing questions. Pro Bono and Law School Clinic programs may provide free legal assistance if eligibility criteria are met. Contact info and hours are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding during and after examination (procedural options)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO provides guidance and initiatives for responding to Office Actions, interviews, appeal options, RCEs, AFCP 2.0, pre-appeal, and actions after allowance or abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resources include sample amendment format, Automated Interview Request (AIR) procedures, Interview practice guidance, types of Office Actions and response submission locations, appeals information (PTAB), After Final Consideration Pilot (AFCP) 2.0 rules, Request for Continued Examination (RCE) filing, and pre-appeal brief requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and signature guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO provides guidance on proper and improper signature examples and instructions for completing Power of Attorney change forms (AIA/80 or AI/81).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow provided examples for proper signatures; use the applicable Power of Attorney forms and follow instructions to change power of attorney.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application completeness and filing date implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Application completeness affects filing date and processing; missing essential filing requirements can trigger Notices which must be corrected to establish the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential filing papers include specification, drawings, and claims. Correcting deficiencies affects the official filing date. See MPEP section 506 for more on completeness and section 509 for fee completeness.
